slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
Three parts. First, naming one commit: by ancestry, by reflog entry, by upstream, by message search, by path.
The method for all the range exercises today is the same: draw the graph, shade the commits you expect, then run the command.
The project is scorekit, a small library that scores model answers against reference answers.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.body: For diff, the analogy is two photographs.
One sentence joins the two: log selects commits, diff selects two trees.

                   /
  ...---ca7e2b7---2652768---e376e5b               main
        (merge base)

  main..feat/report    = { a8e8550, f37a7d8, a10f9a1 }                    what the branch has that main lacks
  feat/report..main    = { 2652768, e376e5b }                             what main has that the branch lacks
  main...feat/report   = { 2652768, e376e5b, a8e8550, f37a7d8, a10f9a1 }  both of the above

  git diff feat/report...main   compares the trees of ca7e2b7 and e376e5b   (merge base and the other tip)

slides.text:
Observed behavior : "git diff main feature" shows a setting being deleted that the feature never touched
Git state         : main gained commits after the branch forked; the feature's tip does not contain them
Mechanism         : A B (and A..B) compare the trees of the two tips, in the direction A to B
Root cause        : what main added after the fork is absent from the feature's tree, so it prints as "-"
Why Git does this : diff takes two endpoints; it does not look at ancestry unless asked (three dots)
Correct fix       : git diff main...feature, or git diff --merge-base main feature
Prevention        : three dots for review; in scripts the explicit --merge-base spelling

items: Reviewing a branch with git diff main feature. Root cause: two endpoints compare the two tips, so everything main gained after the fork appears reversed, as deletions by the feature.
Reading A..B in git diff as a range of commits. Root cause: diff compares two trees; the dots are a spelling of two endpoints, not a set.
Thinking of A..B in git log as "the commits between A and B". Root cause: a range is defined by reachability, and with merges it can contain commits older than A.
Using main@{yesterday} in a script or in a message to a colleague. Root cause: reflog forms read the local reflog; the same text names another commit, or nothing, in another clone.
Using :/text to find "the" commit. Root cause: it returns the youngest match reachable from any ref, which may be a copy on another branch; <rev>^{/text} restricts the search.

slides.body: Before a push, git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD is "what am I about to publish".
And in scripts, write the explicit --merge-base spelling instead of three dots, so that the next reader does not have to remember which meaning the dots have here.

Today the dots stopped being a guess.

beats.text: The reviewer ran git diff main feat/report. The pull request page shows something else. Both are diffs of "the branch against main". They differ by one dot, and that dot decides which two snapshots are compared.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. For twenty videos you've been typing things like main..HEAD, HEAD~2, @{u}, ORIG_HEAD, feat/x@{1}. Each one names a commit, one saved snapshot of the project, or a set of commits. This video collects them into a system, because every investigation command in the next module takes them as arguments.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. For twenty videos you've been typing things like `main..HEAD`, `HEAD~2`, `@{u}`, `ORIG_HEAD`, `feat/x@{1}`. Each one names a commit, one saved snapshot of the project, or a set of commits. This video collects them into a system, because every investigation command in the next module takes them as arguments.

beats.text: Three parts. First, naming one commit: by ancestry, by reflog entry, by upstream, by message search, by path. Second, naming sets of commits: what A..B and A...B select in git log. Third, what git diff does with the same text, which is not the same thing, and which of the two forms a pull request shows.
beats.tele: Three parts. First, naming one commit: by ancestry, by reflog entry, by upstream, by message search, by path. Second, naming sets of commits: what `A..B` and `A...B` select in `git log`. Third, what `git diff` does with the same text, which is not the same thing, and which of the two forms a pull request shows.

beats.text: The method for all the range exercises today is the same: draw the graph, shade the commits you expect, then run the command.
beats.tele: The method for all the range exercises today is the same: draw the graph, shade the commits you expect, then run the command.

beats.text: The project is scorekit, a small library that scores model answers against reference answers. Its history was prepared for the investigation chapter, and you'll use it through the whole next module.

beats.text: Here's what you'll walk away with.

beats.text: After this video you can:
beats.tele: After this video you can:

beats.text: Name a commit by ancestry, by reflog entry, by upstream, by message search and by path.
beats.tele: Name a commit by ancestry, by reflog entry, by upstream, by message search and by path.

beats.text: State what A..B and A...B select in git log.
beats.tele: State what `A..B` and `A...B` select in `git log`.

beats.text: State what A..B and A...B compare in git diff, and why the dots mean something else there.
beats.tele: State what `A..B` and `A...B` compare in `git diff`, and why the dots mean something else there.

beats.text: Choose the diff form that matches what a pull request shows.
beats.tele: Choose the diff form that matches what a pull request shows.

beats.text: Predict log and diff output from a drawn graph.
beats.tele: Predict log and diff output from a drawn graph.

beats.text: Naming one commit.
beats.tele: Naming one commit.

beats.text: Read the third column. It tells you how far to trust each name. Names read from the graph and from objects mean the same in every clone. Names read from your reflog, the local list of where each ref has been, mean something only in your repository. @{u} depends on your configuration.

beats.text: Naming sets of commits. In one sentence: a range is a set of commits defined by reachability: everything you can reach from the included tips, minus everything you can reach from the excluded ones. Reaching means following parent links. On screen, today's graph: main has two commits of its own, feat/report has three, and ca7e2b7 is their merge base, the most recent commit both contain.
beats.tele: Naming sets of commits. In one sentence: a range is a set of commits defined by reachability: everything you can reach from the included tips, minus everything you can reach from the excluded ones. Reaching means following parent links. On screen, today's graph: `main` has two commits of its own, `feat/report` has three, and `ca7e2b7` is their merge base, the most recent commit both contain.

beats.text: For history-walking commands, one revision means "this commit and all its ancestors", and several revisions mean the union. A leading caret excludes a commit and its ancestors. The dotted forms are shorthands.
beats.tele: For history-walking commands, one revision means "this commit and all its ancestors", and several revisions mean the union. A leading caret excludes a commit and its ancestors. The dotted forms are shorthands.

beats.text: An omitted side means HEAD: origin/main.. is origin/main..HEAD.
beats.tele: An omitted side means HEAD: `origin/main..` is `origin/main..HEAD`.

beats.text: Diff. In one sentence: git diff 🟢 SAFE compares exactly two snapshots, and every form of the command differs only in which two it picks.
beats.tele: Diff. In one sentence: `git diff` 🟢 SAFE compares exactly two snapshots, and every form of the command differs only in which two it picks.

beats.text: The manual is blunt about the dots: "diff is about comparing two endpoints, not ranges", and the range notations do not mean a range as defined in the section on specifying ranges. The textbook adds that the two meanings are among the most common misreadings of Git. So if the dots have confused you, you're in large company.
beats.tele: The manual is blunt about the dots: "diff is about comparing two endpoints, not ranges", and the range notations do not mean a range as defined in the section on specifying ranges. The textbook adds that the two meanings are among the most common misreadings of Git. So if the dots have confused you, you're in large company.

beats.text: So, the two sentences to keep. In git log, two dots mean "reachable from B and not from A", and three dots mean the symmetric difference: reachable from one of them, not from both. In git diff, two dots compare the two endpoints, and three dots compare the merge base with B.
beats.tele: So, the two sentences to keep. In `git log`, two dots mean "reachable from B and not from A", and three dots mean the symmetric difference: reachable from one of them, not from both. In `git diff`, two dots compare the two endpoints, and three dots compare the merge base with B.

beats.text: Inside .git, none of this writes anything. Every command in this video is 🟢 SAFE.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`, none of this writes anything. Every command in this video is 🟢 SAFE.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy for ranges: colour every commit reachable from B green, then colour every commit reachable from A red, red winning. A..B is what stays green.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy for ranges: colour every commit reachable from B green, then colour every commit reachable from A red, red winning. `A..B` is what stays green.

beats.text: Try it on the picture, with main as A and feat/report as B: three commits stay green.
beats.tele: Try it on the picture, with `main` as A and `feat/report` as B: three commits stay green.

beats.text: The picture breaks if you think of "between": a range is not an interval on a line, and with merges in the graph the green set can contain commits made long before A.
beats.tele: The picture breaks if you think of "between": a range is not an interval on a line, and with merges in the graph the green set can contain commits made long before A.

beats.text: For diff, the analogy is two photographs. A diff is the comparison of two photographs. It's not the film between them: whatever happened in between, and in which order, is invisible. It breaks at one form. A...B chooses its first photograph by consulting the commit graph, so the same two branch names can give a different diff next week, after one of them has moved or been merged.
beats.tele: For diff, the analogy is two photographs. A diff is the comparison of two photographs. It's not the film between them: whatever happened in between, and in which order, is invisible. It breaks at one form. `A...B` chooses its first photograph by consulting the commit graph, so the same two branch names can give a different diff next week, after one of them has moved or been merged.

beats.text: One sentence joins the two: log selects commits, diff selects two trees. If you catch yourself asking "which commits does this diff cover", you have mixed the models.
beats.tele: One sentence joins the two: log selects commits, diff selects two trees. If you catch yourself asking "which commits does this diff cover", you have mixed the models.

beats.text: One graph, for both halves. The three log lines each select a set of commits. The three diff lines each compare two trees. Pause here if you like, and check each line against the graph.
beats.tele: One graph, for both halves. The three log lines each select a set of commits. The three diff lines each compare two trees. Pause here if you like, and check each line against the graph.

beats.text: Part 1: naming one commit.
beats.tele: Part 1: naming one commit.

beats.text: HEAD~1, HEAD~2, and HEAD^, which is the same commit as HEAD~1. The difference between the tilde and the caret shows on merges. 8657273 is a merge commit, a commit with two parents. Quick quiz, three options. Which two name the same commit? Option one: ^1 and ~1. Option two: ~1 and ^2. Option three: ^1 and ^2. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: `HEAD~1`, `HEAD~2`, and `HEAD^`, which is the same commit as `HEAD~1`. The difference between the tilde and the caret shows on merges. `8657273` is a merge commit, a commit with two parents. Quick quiz, three options. Which two name the same commit? Option one: `^1` and `~1`. Option two: `~1` and `^2`. Option three: `^1` and `^2`. Say it out loud.

beats.text: Option one. ^1 and ~1 are the same commit, the first parent, which is the branch that was merged into. On screen that's 389337a. ^2 is the tip of the branch that was merged in, c0d33a5, and ^2~1 walks one step back on that side. The caret chooses among parents. The tilde walks generations along first parents.

On screen that's `389337a`. `^2` is the tip of the branch that was merged in, `c0d33a5`, and `^2~1` walks one step back on that side. The caret chooses among parents. The tilde walks generations along first parents.

beats.text: The reflog forms read your local reflog and nothing else. main@{yesterday} does not mean "the commit made yesterday". It means "what main pointed at in this clone 24 hours ago", here a commit from Monday 12:31, because the lab clock stands at Tuesday shortly before 13:00. On a teammate's machine, or in a fresh clone whose reflog starts today, the same expression gives a different answer or a warning. Use reflog forms to investigate your own repository. Use dates with git log --since to investigate the project.

Use dates with `git log --since` to investigate the project.

beats.text: @{u} resolves through the upstream configuration: the branch on the server that yours follows. @{u}.. is then "my commits that the remote-tracking branch does not have".
beats.tele: `@{u}` resolves through the upstream configuration: the branch on the server that yours follows. `@{u}..` is then "my commits that the remote-tracking branch does not have".

beats.text: Searching by message. :/nightly run matches two commits in this repository, the original on feat/report and its copy on main. The rule "youngest, from any ref" picked the copy. <rev>^{/<text>} restricts the search to the ancestors of one revision and is the form to use in scripts.
beats.tele: Searching by message. `:/nightly run` matches two commits in this repository, the original on `feat/report` and its copy on `main`. The rule "youngest, from any ref" picked the copy. `<rev>^{/<text>}` restricts the search to the ancestors of one revision and is the form to use in scripts.

beats.text: An annotated tag is an object of its own, so the tag name and the commit it marks have different IDs: the first line is the tag object, the second and third are the commit, the fourth is its tree. ^{} peels. You need the suffix when you compare IDs, as in "is the tag still on the commit we deployed".
beats.tele: An annotated tag is an object of its own, so the tag name and the commit it marks have different IDs: the first line is the tag object, the second and third are the commit, the fourth is its tree. `^{}` peels. You need the suffix when you compare IDs, as in "is the tag still on the commit we deployed".

beats.text: Paths select inside a revision: a blob in main, the same path in v0.1.0, and with a leading colon alone, the index entry. git show v0.1.0:scorekit/config.py prints a file from a release without any checkout.
beats.tele: Paths select inside a revision: a blob in `main`, the same path in `v0.1.0`, and with a leading colon alone, the index entry. `git show v0.1.0:scorekit/config.py` prints a file from a release without any checkout.

beats.text: And when a name resolves to nothing, Git says so: a path that did not exist at that revision, a tag that does not exist.
beats.tele: And when a name resolves to nothing, Git says so: a path that did not exist at that revision, a tag that does not exist.

beats.text: Part 2: ranges in git log. labs/run ch14a/ranges. Use the diagram. Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: draw this graph, and for main..feat/report, shade the commits you expect.
beats.tele: Part 2: ranges in `git log`. `labs/run ch14a/ranges`. Use the diagram. Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: draw this graph, and for `main..feat/report`, shade the commits you expect.

beats.text: Three commits, and three spellings of the same set: two dots, a leading caret, and --not.
beats.tele: Three commits, and three spellings of the same set: two dots, a leading caret, and `--not`.

beats.text: The mirror image: two commits.
beats.tele: The mirror image: two commits.

beats.text: Now three dots. Shade first. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Now three dots. Shade first. I'll wait.

beats.text: Five commits: the union of the two.
beats.tele: Five commits: the union of the two.

beats.text: --left-right says which side each commit is on, and --boundary adds the commit where the walk stopped, marked with an o: the merge base, ca7e2b7.
beats.tele: `--left-right` says which side each commit is on, and `--boundary` adds the commit where the walk stopped, marked with an `o`: the merge base, `ca7e2b7`.

beats.text: The parent shorthands, on the merge commit. ^@ is both parents. ^! is the commit alone. And 8657273^- is the answer to "what did this merge bring in": the merge itself and the two commits of the side branch.
beats.tele: The parent shorthands, on the merge commit. `^@` is both parents. `^!` is the commit alone. And `8657273^-` is the answer to "what did this merge bring in": the merge itself and the two commits of the side branch.

beats.text: For an ordinary commit, A^! gives git diff the pair that git show uses.
beats.tele: For an ordinary commit, `A^!` gives `git diff` the pair that `git show` uses.

beats.text: An empty A..B means B is an ancestor of A, which is the test git merge-base --is-ancestor performs.
beats.tele: An empty `A..B` means B is an ancestor of A, which is the test `git merge-base --is-ancestor` performs.

beats.text: And one query lists all unmerged work in a repository: --branches --not main. Look at the last three lines of that list. feat/rouge-l appears although its content is on main: it was squash-merged, and a squash creates a new commit that has no parent link to the branch. The graph knows ancestry, not content. You've met that sentence in four different videos now.

Look at the last three lines of that list. `feat/rouge-l` appears although its content is on `main`: it was squash-merged, and a squash creates a new commit that has no parent link to the branch. beats.text: Part 3: the same dots in git diff. labs/run ch14a/diff-endpoints.

beats.text: The graph of the diagram. The branch has three commits of its own, main has two, and the merge base is ca7e2b7. Two endpoints, with and without the two dots:
beats.tele: The graph of the diagram. The branch has three commits of its own, `main` has two, and the merge base is `ca7e2b7`. Two endpoints, with and without the two dots:

beats.text: Identical. Three files, and one of them is scorekit/config.py with a deletion. Now three dots. Predict which files are listed. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Identical. Three files, and one of them is `scorekit/config.py` with a deletion. Now three dots. Predict which files are listed. I'll wait.

beats.text: config.py is gone from the list, and README.md has appeared. The second command spells the same comparison out with git merge-base. The two results disagree about two files, and each disagreement is worth reading.
beats.tele: `config.py` is gone from the list, and `README.md` has appeared. The second command spells the same comparison out with `git merge-base`. The two results disagree about two files, and each disagreement is worth reading.

beats.text: That's the opening story. feat/report never touched scorekit/config.py. main added a line after the fork. Going from the tree of main to the tree of the branch, that line is absent, so the two-endpoint diff prints it as a deletion. The reviewer compared tips and read main's own progress, reversed, as part of the feature. Almost every reviewer types that command once. With three dots: no output.
beats.tele: That's the opening story. `feat/report` never touched `scorekit/config.py`. `main` added a line after the fork. Going from the tree of `main` to the tree of the branch, that line is absent, so the two-endpoint diff prints it as a deletion. The reviewer compared tips and read `main`'s own progress, reversed, as part of the feature. Almost every reviewer types that command once. With three dots: no output.

beats.text: The README paragraph is the opposite case. It was written on the branch and then cherry-picked to main. Both tips contain it, so the tips don't differ. The merge base does not contain it, so the three-dot diff shows it as a change of the branch, although main already has it.
beats.tele: The README paragraph is the opposite case. It was written on the branch and then cherry-picked to `main`. Both tips contain it, so the tips don't differ. The merge base does not contain it, so the three-dot diff shows it as a change of the branch, although `main` already has it.

beats.text: Swap the operands and the three-dot form compares the merge base with the other tip: what main did since the fork.
beats.tele: Swap the operands and the three-dot form compares the merge base with the other tip: what `main` did since the fork.

beats.text: One more form, useful in forensics: the operands may be trees or blobs, addressed as <rev>:<path>.
beats.tele: One more form, useful in forensics: the operands may be trees or blobs, addressed as `<rev>:<path>`.

beats.text: A directory compared between a release tag and main, and then one file. No checkout is needed.
beats.tele: A directory compared between a release tag and `main`, and then one file. No checkout is needed.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Reviewing a branch with git diff main feature. Root cause: two endpoints compare the two tips, so everything main gained after the fork appears reversed, as deletions by the feature.
beats.tele: Reviewing a branch with `git diff main feature`. Root cause: two endpoints compare the two tips, so everything `main` gained after the fork appears reversed, as deletions by the feature.

beats.text: Reading A..B in git diff as a range of commits. Root cause: diff compares two trees; the dots are a spelling of two endpoints, not a set.

beats.text: The "Files changed" tab of a pull request, GitHub's proposal to merge one branch into another, shows a three-dot diff, from the merge base to the head of the pull request branch, according to GitHub's documentation. beats.text: In git log, A..B is what is reachable from B and not from A, and A...B is what is reachable from exactly one of them. In git diff, A..B compares the two tips and A...B compares the merge base with B. For review I use three dots, which is what a pull request shows. A range is a set by reachability, not an interval.
